title: On the Impact of Extra Information in Bandit Learning: More is Not Always Merrier
claim: More free, unbiased side information can hurt one learning algorithm while helping another, and the contrast holds across difficulty levels.
layout: 3 line-plot panels, left-to-right, shared regret axis with shaded confidence bands
description: Three side-by-side line plots with a regret y-axis and shaded confidence bands. Panel (a), titled UCB1, plots regret against time for D^0 (blue), D^1 (green) and D^2 (red). The blue curve with no extra information sits clearly lowest, ending near 28, while the green and red curves end near 34 and 36. Panel (b), titled Thompson Sampling, uses the same layout, but the order is reversed: red (D^2) is lowest, near 31, and blue is highest, near 35. Panel (c), titled Variation with Sub-optimality Gap, plots regret against gap Δ from 0.01 to 0.4. Solid lines show D^0 and dotted lines show D^1, for UCB (blue) and Thompson Sampling (green). The dotted blue UCB D^1 curve peaks near 125 at small gaps, far above the other curves. Captions (a)–(c) sit below the panels.
caption: We compare the Upper Confidence Bound algorithm ($\ucb$) and the Thompson Sampling ($\ts$) algorithm on a two-armed bandit instance with action mean rewards $\mu=\left( \nicefrac{1}{2}+\Delta,\nicefrac{1}{2} \right)$ and $\Delta=0.1$ under three extra-information designs, where $\dd^i$ provides $i$ additional unbiased, independent samples of the optimal action at each time step. [ref] shows increasing extra information consistently increases the regret of $\ucb$, while [ref] shows monotone regret reduction for Thompson Sampling. [ref] demonstrates that this qualitative contrast persists across different gaps $\Delta$, with larger regret increase for $\ucb$ on harder (smaller-gap) instances.
abstract: More data is commonly assumed to improve learning performance, however, we show that this intuition can surprisngly fail in sequential decision-making. Considering a stochastic bandits setup with exogenous extra information, we ask if the free and unbiased extra reward samples are guaranteed to reduce the regret of the learner. We introduce a formal notion of `non-degradation under extra information' and demonstrate that the widely used Upper Confidence Bound algorithm (UCB) violates this property, i.e., there exist benign extra-information under which UCB incurs strictly higher regret than when run without extra information. We contrast this behaviour with Thompson Sampling and Explore-Then-Commit, which appear to benefit from the same extra information. Constructively, we propose a meta-algorithm that provably enforces non-degradation for a broad class of bandit algorithms. We also run empirical simulations to study our meta-algorithm.
